### Intent
> Section 3 of the /deeper design: a step in the home skill's brief writing, not a separate file. It runs on its own for research, perf, analysis and outcome briefs, with its own copy of the four questions. Answer 2 goes to the scout's `Read:` or the request's sources, answer 3 goes in the brief for the crew, and answer 4 goes in `Proves it:`. Mechanical fixes, docs changes and bug fixes with a known cause skip it. `/deeper` stays manual.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings
- Reviewer B: 7 findings
- They agreed on the four central issues and diverged only in severity and in a few single-reviewer nits. Both were asked the review skill's questions.

### Act On

**1. The step writes brief lines the template forbids or never defines** (A1, B1)
The step tells the home to put a `Read:` line (answer 2) and an `Instruments:` line (answer 3) on briefs it writes itself.
- `templates/brief.md:17` says home-written briefs leave `Read:` out.
- `Instruments:` is defined nowhere: not in the template, the crew skill, the scout skill or the parser.
- The step's own wording, "though the home wrote it", admits the conflict without resolving it.
- A scout following `skills/scout/SKILL.md:125` drops answer 3 entirely.

The template is under "Do not touch", so the fix belongs in this PR's text:
- Put answer 3 in a line the brief already has, such as the task body or the Done-when list, as the "Done when" asks.
- Put answer 2 in `Read:` only where a scout writes the brief. That case is the one the "Done when" actually names, and the template already allows it.

If a dedicated `Instruments:` line is still wanted, record it in the Result as a follow-up for `templates/brief.md` and the scout skill.

**2. The step is keyed on the playbook name, not on the kind of work** (A2, B2, A3, A4, B3)
These five findings share one root cause, and fixing it resolves all of them:
- `bug-fix` always skips, although its playbook covers bugs whose cause is unknown. The principle exempts only proven-cause fixes. The test `test_a_mechanical_fix_a_docs_change_and_a_known_bug_skip_it` pins the wrong behaviour in place.
- Outcome work under `feature` or `autonomous-run` always skips. That breaks the intent's "outcome briefs".
- For a scout request, the step is decided by the scout's own playbook, which is always `investigation` or `trace-forensics`. So the four questions get pushed onto requests that brief docs or known-cause fixes. That breaks "Done when" line 2.
- The hand-kept list of ten playbook names drifts silently, and the test checks only one direction.

Fix: make the stated kind of the task being briefed the case input every time, e.g. `research|perf|analysis|outcome|known-cause-fix|mechanical|docs`. The playbook may suggest a default, but it does not decide. This deletes the name list rather than maintaining it, and it is the "code judo" move. Then update the skip test so it pins the kinds, with an unknown-cause bug fix running the step.

**3. `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` are not shown** (B7)
These are "Done when" lines. Neither reviewer could verify them, and the fixes above change the text and the tests anyway. Run both after the fixes and put their output in the Result. The Result must also say how the "Proves it" brief was checked before the merge. Neither reviewer noticed this second gap, but it is part of the same "Done when".

### Consider

- **A request with no brief in its Deliver list loses answers 3 and 4** (A5, B4). The step works out the answers, then has nowhere to put them. B's remedy is cheap and uses lines the request template already has: write them as `Questions:` items. That also replaces the ad-hoc packing of methods and the judge into the Deliver bullet. The tradeoff is one sentence of text for a path that may be rare.
- **The "Done when already names its data, instruments and judge" skip lives only in prose** (B6). The block prints `deeper` and the trailing sentence then overrides it. With the kind-based input from Act On 2, this can become one more kind so the block prints the skip itself. Do it if it falls out naturally from that rewrite.
- **No test ties the named brief lines to the templates** (A6). Once Act On 1 fixes the destinations, an executing test that checks each line the block echoes against `templates/brief.md` and `templates/scout-request.md` would have caught finding 1. It is worth adding with that fix.

### Noted

- **"The block under it" in durable-scout step 1 points about 90 lines away into another section** (B5). Naming the section is a one-word clarity fix. It is cheap enough to do while editing that line, but it is not a blocker.

### Dismissed

None. Every finding was either real or a facet of a real one. The reviewers did not inflate nits.

### Agreement Map

The reviewers converged independently on the same two structural problems:
- The step sends answers to lines the brief contract does not hold.
- The step classifies work by playbook name instead of by kind.

That consensus is a strong signal. The divergences were in coverage, not in disagreement:
- A alone caught the scout-request misclassification (A3).
- B alone caught the prose-only skip, the dangling reference, and the unverified `make check`.

Most of the findings trace back to one design choice: using the playbook name as a stand-in for the kind of work. Replacing that stand-in with the real input removes five findings and a maintained list in one move.

### Intent
> Add a `Proves it:` line to `templates/brief.md`, right after `Done when:`. The brief parser (`src/jbriefs/parse.py`) and jbus's pre-launch brief checks (beside `dispatch.designed`) accept it only when it names something outside the agent: a test, metric, dataset, external judge or the user. They refuse an empty line, the template text, and any proof by the crew, crewmate, reviewer, agent, "self", "the model" or a review alone, each with a one-line reason. Briefs that lack the line are handled the way the Design line was introduced: the Result states whether existing queued briefs are refused or grandfathered, without stranding an approved row. The change includes tests for every accepted and refused kind, home-skill and docs updates, and a green `make check`.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings
- The two reviewers agreed on five of their findings, and A's grandfathering finding stands alone. Both answered the review skill's questions.

### Act On

**1. The "outside" patterns are loose, and because they are checked before `_SELF`, self-referential proofs pass** (A1, B1, B2)
`proof()` returns success on the first `_OUTSIDE` match. Several of those patterns match ordinary words:
- any backticked span
- `make \w`, which matches "make sure"
- `\btests?\b`, which matches "self-test"
- a bare `%`
- `\bjudge\b`
- `his word`
- `evals`

So these lines all launch:
- "the crewmate will make sure it works"
- "the reviewer is 100% sure"
- "the model is the judge"
- "`self`"

Both reviewers built concrete lines that pass. This gate is the only check before `_ready` launches, and the task names exactly these phrasings as ones to refuse. The tests only pin the happy side of the precedence rule (B2): no refused case contains a trigger token.

Fix:
- Make the outside patterns specific: a test path or name, a backticked command naming a known tool, `make <target>` but not "make sure", `%` only near a metric word, and "the user"/"the operator" rather than "his …".
- Add a `REFUSED` case for each example above, and have each case execute `parse.proof`.

**2. Missing `Proves it:` is exempt forever, not only for briefs queued before this change** (A2)
`proven()` returns `""` whenever `proves_it` returns None, so a brief written tomorrow without the line launches ungated. The Done-when line asks for a choice about *existing queued* briefs. As built, the parser's "requires it" holds only through prose in the home skill, and `docs/jbus.md:85` asserts an assumption the code never checks.

Fix: tie the exemption to something the queue already records, such as the row's `approved` time or `brief_sha` against a cut-off, and gate on anything approved later. Approved rows stay unstranded and the bypass closes. This comes from one reviewer, but the execution path is concrete and it defeats the point of the task.

### Consider

**3. A brief that fails both checks raises two gates in sequence** (A3)
`proven` runs only when `designed` passes. A brief that fails both therefore costs the user two edit-and-approve rounds. Joining both faults into one gate keyed by the brief sha is a small change and removes the `short, kind` juggling. It is not a correctness bug, but every round is the user's time.

**4. `Brief.proof` (and `Proof.said`) have no consumer outside the tests** (A5, B4)
Both reviewers found the same unused surface. Either drop the property or show it on the jbriefs page. The fix is cheap, and the cost of leaving it is low.

**5. The template text is detected by a leading `<`** (A6, B5)
This fails both ways:
- A genuine line like `<= 50 ms p95 from jgauge` is refused.
- The guide text with its brackets stripped is accepted, because it contains "test".

Matching `^<[^>]*>$` or comparing against the template's own line would be exact. The tightened test pattern from item 1 largely closes A6's side. B5's false refusal is rare but real, and refusing "the template's own text" is a Done-when line.

### Noted

- **Duplicate head-scanning loop in `proves_it` and `designed`; `proven` is a pass-through** (A4, B3). This is real duplication. The shared `head_line` helper, though, means moving `designed`, which is existing code in a "do not touch" area. Note it for later. A `(kind, check)` tuple loop in `_ready` is premature with only two checks. If item 3 is taken, `_ready` gets simpler anyway.
- **Two Done-when items cannot be verified from the diff** (A7, B6): the Result's grandfather-or-refuse statement, and the printed run of one real queued brief through the launch check. Confirm both in the brief's Result. If item 2 changes the grandfathering rule, the Result must state the new rule.

### Dismissed

None. Every finding pointed at a concrete line or a real gap.

### Agreement Map

The reviewers converged on every structural point: the loose `_OUTSIDE` patterns, the duplicated loop, the dead `Brief.proof` property, the `<` heuristic, and the unverifiable Result items. B rated the pattern problem critical and A rated it a warning, but both built working bypass lines, so the consensus is strong. A alone looked at the gate's *lifecycle*: the permanent exemption for briefs with no line, and the sequential double gate. That lifecycle angle produced one of the two must-fix items. The pattern says the regex core is the weak spot, and its tests mirror its own assumptions. B's B2 explains why A1/B1 got through: the tests were written from the patterns rather than against them.

### Intent
> Task P7 of the pstack catch-up audit. Answer from the code whether jmerge's "fails over today's main" check runs the checks on the merge result. If it does, record that in THIRD_PARTY.md. If it does not, make it re-check when main changed a caller or a dependency of the PR's files (or a lockfile), with a test. Answer from T3's own tool schema whether a `modelSelection` launch takes an effort setting, and write the decision in THIRD_PARTY.md. Never set effort above medium. `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` pass. Proof: the merge-result test, and the T3 schema quoted in the Result.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings (4 warnings, 3 nits)
- Reviewer B: 5 findings (4 warnings, 1 nit)
- They agreed on two warnings: the unproven effort shape and the missed bare-name imports. They also agreed on the per-file subprocess cost.

### Act On

1. **The effort `options` shape is asserted but not shown by T3's schema, and no test pins it** (A1, B4). The fixture types `options` as `anyOf [{}, null]`, so the schema test passes any shape. "Proves it" requires quoting the T3 schema, and this schema cannot prove the answer. If the shape is wrong, T3 may silently drop the option and every Claude role launches at `high`. That breaks the user's hard rule while looking compliant. Both reviewers raised it independently.
   - Find the real source (T3's provider or model-options code, or a captured accepted launch) and cite it in THIRD_PARTY.md.
   - Pin the shape in a fixture and test against it.
   - If no source can be found, record the question as a `jbus gate`.

2. **The rule is claimed for every role, but Codex and Grok lines send no effort and their defaults were never checked** (A2). THIRD_PARTY.md and the module docstring make a claim the PR did not verify, and a `crew: codex …` line could run above medium. The cheap fix is within scope:
   - Narrow both texts to Claude lines.
   - Gate the Codex/Grok default question.
   - Capping those providers can be a later task.

3. **A rename leaves callers of the old path unseen** (B1). `left` reaches `stale_paths` but not `related`, and GitHub lists only the new path. The concrete path is: the PR moves `core.py` to `engine.py`, then main adds `from pkg import core`, and the check stays green while the merge result has a broken import. That is the central #613 case, and the test only covers an in-place rename. The fix is small: feed `left` into `ours` with empty text, and add a `git mv` Kitchen test.

4. **Bare-name sibling imports in `tests/` are never matched** (A4, B2). `modules()` only produces dotted and `src`-stripped names. This repo's tests import siblings by bare name, including the PR's own `test_jmerge_callers.py` importing from `test_jmerge_fresh`. So the check misses a real dependency change in this repo. Both reviewers found it independently. Add bare names for files in pytest import roots, plus a test for the sibling case.

5. **The check fails open when the PR head cannot be read in the main checkout** (A3). `git show {head}:{path}` returns empty text, so the "main changed a dependency" direction can never match. `moved` fetches branches only, not `refs/pull/<n>/head`. Every other git failure in jmerge blocks the merge, so this one should too. The fix:
   - Check `cat-file -e`, fetching the PR ref if needed, as `cli.py` already does elsewhere.
   - Treat a head that still cannot be read as stale.
   - Add a test for the missing-head case.

### Consider

- **A path named in prose counts as a dependency** (B3). Docs PRs, this one included, go stale whenever main touches a path they mention, which causes reruns or "needs a rebase" on guarded PRs. It fails closed, so it is safe, but it is noisy. Restricting the path match to code, Makefile and CI files is cheap. The tradeoff is that a narrower match could miss a config file that names a path. My recommendation is to restrict it, but it is not blocking.
- **Three doc files are outside "Where"** (A7): `docs/configuration.md`, `docs/jmerge.md` and `docs/jroles.md`. The edits describe the new behaviour accurately, and dropping them would leave the docs wrong. Keep them, and name them in the Result so whoever owns "Where" can object.

### Noted

- One `git show` per file and quadratic `ast.parse` per pair, per ready PR, per pass (A6, B5). This is real against the 300 s budget at scale, but is not shown to bite today. Batching with `cat-file --batch` and parsing once per file is a good follow-up.
- Plain-substring path matching and the `endswith("conftest.py")` suffix test (A5). This fails closed, and it is mostly subsumed if B3's restriction lands. Switching to a basename check costs one line and can ride along if the code is touched.

### Dismissed

- None. No finding was wrong or a matter of taste. Both reviewers worked from concrete execution paths.

### Agreement Map

- **Agreement:** The reviewers converged on the two weakest points of the PR:
  - The effort answer is not grounded in a schema that actually says it.
  - The import heuristic is tuned to the `src/` layout and ignores how this repo's own tests import.
- **Divergence:** Each found a different hole in the same `related`/`modules` logic. A found the fail-open unreadable head, and B found the dropped `left` paths. Together they suggest the new dependency check was tested only on its happy path (in-place edits under `src/`).
- **Line numbers differ** for the same code (`ready.py:210` vs `868`, `cli.py:169` vs `659`). They likely read hunk-relative versus file positions, but they describe the same functions.
- **Effort-rule exposure:** The non-merge risk all sits in the effort decision, where an unverified shape plus unchecked providers could quietly break the user's "never above medium" rule. That is why it leads the list.

### Intent
> Replace the two pr-review reviewer subagents (A/B) per pull request with one scoped review thread. That thread reads only the diff, posts one combined review, and writes one `## Review` section that jmerge's ready rule still accepts (`Reviewers: 1`). jbus archives that review thread on the next pass after the PR merges or closes, and never archives one whose PR is still open. Every skill or doc that says "two reviewers" now says one. Tests cover: the skill names no A/B call, merged versus open archive behaviour, and the new section read as ready. `make check` exits 0.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 4 findings
- They agreed on three points: the archive's "closed" rule is unsound (A2/B1), Step 4's "not given" claim is stale (A6/B2), and some files are outside `Where` (A7/B4). Both answered the review skill's questions.

### Act On
- **Unreliable "closed" detection drives an archive** (A2, B1). `shut()` calls a PR closed when its URL is missing from a 100-item open list, matched as a raw string. It never reads the real state, and it disagrees with `watch.pull()`, which already decides closed or merged. Any open PR that lands outside that list, or whose URL has a different form, gets its review thread archived. That breaks the Done-when line "a review thread of an open pull request is never archived", and jbus never undoes an archive.
  - Fix: use the existing `pull(...) in (MERGED, CLOSED)` rule, so closed is defined in one place.
  - Add a test for an open PR that is missing from `open.json`.
- **The jmerge new-shape test has no finding in it** (A1). The template's `Findings:` line has nothing after the colon, so the fill logic skips it and the section reaches `ready.py` with `found == 0`. The rule "findings answered" is never exercised.
  - Fix: write a real `- warning ...` item into the section.
  - Add a negative case, the same section with no `Finding:` line, which must not be ready. This is the Done-when test, so it must test the real thing.
- **`docs/flow.html:214` still says "Two reviewers ... settles itself"** (A3). A Done-when line names this case explicitly. The page is hand-written and not covered by the docs sweep, so nothing else will catch it.
- **Step 4 claims the lead has context the reading lacked** (A6, B2). `skills/pr-review/SKILL.md:232` is left over from the two-subagent design. In one thread, the reading already has the brief's decisions, so the skill now promises the reviewer an independent cross-check that does not exist.
  - Fix: say that the judgment re-checks each claim against the repo and the brief.
  - Both reviewers raised it, the skill text is the deliverable, and the fix is one sentence.

### Consider
- **The `"archive"` key in a prefix-keyed map** (A4). It is a mode flag inside a map of title prefixes, and it brings a special case, `shelve` propagation, and a nested loop with `break`. Computing `ended` once in `settle` and deriving the action at the call site would delete all of that.
  - Tradeoff: it is not a bug. But the fix for A2/B1 already rewrites this area, so doing both at once costs little.
- **A merged PR whose last Review is `not run` never gets archived** (A5). `archive = reviewed & ended` requires a clean or findings verdict, so a later `not run` pass keeps all review threads forever, including the first one that finished cleanly. The Done-when line says archive on merge.

1. First, before adding the fifth kind, replace the silent `default: break;` with an exhaustiveness guard. Otherwise the new variant falls through unhandled and the compiler stays quiet.
2. I follow **"Exhaustive matching is the compiler's job"**: use a `never`-typed binding in TypeScript.
3. I write: `default: { const _exhaustive: never = event; throw new Error(\`unhandled event kind: ${(_exhaustive as { kind: string }).kind}\`); }`
4. Then I add the fifth kind to the union and run `npx tsc --noEmit`. It should fail at that `default`, which confirms the guard works.
5. I add an explicit `case` for the new kind, plus a deliberate no-op case for any kinds that really should do nothing, and re-run `npx tsc --noEmit` until it is clean.
6. I grep for other `switch (*.kind)` sites with the same `default: break;` pattern (`rg "default:\s*break" -t ts`) and guard those too.

### Intent
> Sections 1, 2, 5 and 6 of the /deeper design, built on Felix Rieseberg's "four types of ambition". This adds four things:
> - a manual `/deeper` skill that answers the four questions and returns a rewritten prompt, which a home takes as the default behind a `jbus gate`;
> - the 25th principle, `depth-over-breadth`, sourced by jdrift as jstack's own;
> - a `THIRD_PARTY.md` credit;
> - a blind, rerunnable eval in `evals/deeper/` over about 10 past briefs, scored by something other than the writing agent. Its committed Result says honestly whether /deeper won.
>
> `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` pass.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 5 findings
- Reviewer B: 8 findings
- They agreed independently on two issues: the raw-sources measure has no control, and the eval wipes its results before running. Each also raised issues the other missed.

### Act On

**1. The eval's verdict "won" is not supported by its own evidence (A1, B1, merged).**
- The rule needs /deeper to lose on none of the three measures. The "proof outside" measure decides that.
- Run 1 lost on outside (4 up, 6 down).
- The only change before run 2 was the output format of the rewritten prompt, from a fence to a block quote. Run 2 then won 8 to 2. Eight of ten cases flipped sign between two runs of what is in effect the same skill.
- A then showed the run-2 rise in outside comes entirely from the backtick branch of `OUTSIDE`. Without that branch both arms score about 0.33. Deeper briefs use more inline code because the skill tells them to name things by path and command.
- So the "won" rests on a measure that rewards formatting, re-run after a loss. This is close to what the brief forbade: "If it did not, say so: that is a finding, not a reason to tune the eval."
- The README contradicts itself: "no effect shown" on outside, yet a Result of "won".
- Fix:
  - Drop the bare-backtick branch, or limit it to commands that are run.
  - Re-score both committed runs. This needs no new model calls.
  - Write the Result as what both runs support. Likely: "won on raw and instruments; proof outside not shown; did not win under the rule."
  - Report that as the finding it is.

**2. "Raw sources" may mostly count the skill's own example list, and the README claims it was controlled for (A2, B2, consensus).**
- Seven of the twelve `RAW` kinds match the words of question 2 of the skill almost exactly.
- `beyond` takes the skill's examples out for instruments only, yet "What holds" claims the control for both.
- Fix: add a raw `beyond` that leaves out the skill's listed kinds, and re-score the committed briefs. If the gap shrinks, say so. Otherwise limit the claim to instruments.

**3. The one documented command deletes the committed results before its first model call (A3, B3, consensus).**
- `write()` calls `rmtree` on `runs/` and `deeper/` first, and writes `key.json` only at the end.
- If any of the 60 calls fails, the result is a partial `runs/` with a stale key. A machine without `claude` fails on the first call.
- After that, `report` refuses to run, and the only recovery is git. This breaks the "rerunnable by one command" Done-when line.
- Fix:
  - Write into a temporary directory and swap it in only after the key is written.
  - Check `shutil.which("claude")` before touching anything.

**4. Redaction fails open (B4).**
- `_private` reads `~/.config` directly and ignores `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, which `jleak`'s own CLI respects.
- If the patterns don't load, it returns `()` without a word.
- Cases, briefs and model outputs then go into a repo meant to be public, with nothing redacted. It's one reviewer and the trigger depends on the environment, but leaking private text into a public repo is the kind of security finding not to wave off.
- Fix: resolve the path the way `jleak.cli` does, and fail when the patterns are missing.

### Consider

- **"Not held" is a phrase count presented as a per-brief fact (A4).** The README's "seven of ten did not hold" is read off a count that:
  - searches the whole brief, not just the Result section;
  - misses "did not hold" and "doesn't hold".

  This is the "how it turned out" part of the eval, so it matters more than a nit. Either scope the search to the Result section and match the variants, or call the column a phrase count.
- **`SELF` matches the bare word "review" (B5).** This penalizes `rs-parallel-reviews` for its subject rather than for who judges the result. It's the same kind of problem as item 1 (a measure reading surface wording), so it's worth fixing during that re-score. It affects only one case.

- Reviewer A: 7 findings (4 warnings, 3 nits)
- Reviewer B: 5 findings (4 warnings, 1 nit)
- They agreed on three issues: the unproven effort shape, bare-name test imports, and per-file subprocess cost. Each also found real issues the other missed. Both answered the review skill's questions. Neither reported on the `make check` / `jgauge` line, so its status is unverified here.

### Act On

1. **The effort shape is asserted, not read from T3's schema** (A1, B4).
   - The repo's T3 schema types `options` as `anyOf [{}, null]`, so the `{"id": "effort", "value": …}` list shape has no source.
   - The schema test passes any shape.
   - This misses the "read from T3's own tool schema" and "Proves it" lines.
   - A wrong shape fails silently into the default the PR itself says is `high`. That breaks the one rule this half of the task exists to keep.
   - Fix: cite the real source (T3's provider or model-options code, or a captured accepted launch) and pin the shape in a test that fails on a different shape. If no source can be found, write the decision as unproven in THIRD_PARTY.md and send it to `jbus gate` as a question.

2. **A rename hides callers of the old module** (B1).
   - `related` builds `ours` from `one.files`, which only lists the new path of a rename. `left` is never passed in.
   - The concrete case: a PR moves `core.py` to `engine.py`, and main adds `from pkg import core`. The check stays green, and main ends up with a broken import.
   - That is exactly the "main changed a caller" case in the Done-when line, and the test does not exercise it.
   - Fix: pass `left` into `related` with empty text, and add a Kitchen test that does a `git mv` while main adds a caller of the old module.

3. **Bare-name sibling imports are invisible** (A4, B2).
   - `modules()` only produces the dotted name and the `src`-stripped name.
   - The repo's tests import each other by bare name, including this PR's own `test_jmerge_callers.py`.
   - So when main changes a shared fixture like `Kitchen`, the check still reads as fresh.
   - Both reviewers found this independently, and it happens in this repo.
   - Fix: also count the bare module name for files in a pytest import root (`tests/`), and add a test for the sibling case.

4. **An unreadable head makes the check fail open** (A3).
   - If `git show <head>:<path>` fails, every own file reads as empty, no dependency can match, and the check stays green.
   - `moved` only fetches branches. Code elsewhere in `cli.py` fetches `refs/pull/<n>/head` when the head is missing.
   - Every other git failure in jmerge blocks the merge, so this silent pass is the wrong direction for a merge gate.
   - Fix: check `cat-file -e` first, fetch the PR ref if needed, and return a blocking reason if the head is still missing. Add a test for that case.

### Consider

- **Codex and Grok lines carry no effort, but the docs say the rule holds for every named role** (A2).
  - Not sending effort is not jroles setting it above medium, so the letter of "nothing raises it" holds.
  - But THIRD_PARTY.md and the docstring claim more than was checked.
  - Cheap remedy: narrow the wording to Claude lines and gate the Codex/Grok defaults question.
  - Researching and capping each provider is more work than the task asked for.
- **A path named in prose counts as a dependency** (B3).
  - Docs-only PRs (including this one) go stale whenever main touches a path they mention.
  - This fails closed, so it is not a correctness bug. The cost is reruns and needless rebase demands for guarded PRs.

   - `at` is the directory's mtime, which does not move when a Report is appended to an existing file.

Line 15 says depth "reaches the same outcome" and breadth "changes the outcome", judged against the "Done when". Line 13's third question ("What says it is done?") is itself a change to the "Done when": it swaps self-assessment for a failing-then-passing test, a measured target or an outside judge. The task was a change of style, not of rule, and the principle now disagrees with the skill it backs and the source it credits. This is a one-word revert. If the reasoning style wants a "why", add it as a clause about the effect: it makes the worker reach for the expert's tools instead of trimming the goal.

"Naming a method without the command that runs it here is still words" (line 7) repeats line 12 and interrupts the digested-input, then self-judge, then three-doors chain. "asks these, after what a top professional would do that is not asked, as four questions…" packs the three-versus-four reconciliation into a mid-sentence clause. ### Intent
> Topic 10, "A way to undo a bad merge into standing.md." The home skill (including `skills/home/scoped-homes.md:7`) and the handoff skill run `jbus snapshot` right after any edit to `$H/standing.md`, so each edit becomes its own commit in `~/.local/state/home` and is pushed. The twice-daily timer stays. `jbus snapshot` gains `--why <text>`, which is appended to the commit message after the time. `docs/state.md` gets an "Undo an edit to standing.md" section covering find (`log -p`), restore (`show <commit>^:<path>`) and re-snapshot with `--why`. Tests run the snapshot and the documented restore in a temporary tree with a bare remote. `make check` exits 0. Size S. Design: one flag and one step.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings
- Reviewer B: 5 findings
- They agreed on four issues: concurrency, the destructive restore, the new handoff duty, and the file outside Where. A also flagged the prose rule and the test helper. B also flagged the test name. Both answered the review skill's questions.

### Act On

**1. No lock around `take` now that snapshots run at arbitrary times** (A1, B1, lock part)
Before this change, one timer was the only caller. Now every home and scoped home also snapshots the same tree, and nothing serializes the runs. Both reviewers traced concrete failure paths, not hypotheticals:
- If a home's run overlaps the 08:30 or 17:30 timer run, one of them fails on `.git/index.lock`. When the timer's run loses, `OnFailure` sends a false `--alarm` to the desk and every project.
- Home A's `git reset -q` can land between home B's `git add -A` and B's `diff --cached`. B then prints "nothing changed" and its edit gets no commit, which breaks the core "Done when" guarantee.

The fix is an exclusive `flock` on a file under `.git`, held across add, commit and push in `take`. It is a few lines in `src/jbus/snapshot.py`, inside Where. Both reviewers proposed it independently.

**2. The documented restore truncates the live `standing.md` before `git show` can fail** (A2, B2)
The shell redirect empties the target file first. `git show` then fails in several ordinary cases:
- `<commit>` is the commit that created the file;
- `<commit>` is the root commit;
- the hash is mistyped or ambiguous.

The doc's very next step tells the user to snapshot, which commits the empty file. The command is a deliverable, so it has to be safe. Fixes:
- Use `git -C ~/.local/state/home restore --source=<commit>^ -- <repo>/standing.md`, which writes nothing on failure. A `> tmp && mv` form also works.
- Add one line on the case where the bad commit created the file.
- Add a test that undoes the edit that created `standing.md`.

**3. Handoff gains a new duty to write standing rules** (A5, B3)
"One it did not write yet goes there now, as one dated line" creates a second place where rules get written. The task did not ask for it, and it contradicts the sentence just before it ("the home wrote it to `standing.md` when it heard it"). Cut it, and keep only the general step: after any edit to `$H/standing.md`, run `jbus snapshot --why ...`. That also fixes the hardcoded `added` that A4 noticed drifting from the other two copies.

### Consider

**4. A `--why` commit is whole-tree, so its message can describe less than it contains** (A3, B1 mixed-commit part)
`git add -A` pulls in briefs, `merge.log`, other repos' trees and so on. If two homes edit the same `standing.md` before either one snapshots, one commit holds both edits under one `--why`, and undoing "the bad one" reverts both.
- Against this: path-limited `log -p` and `show` still isolate the file, so the undo still works. Once the lock is in place, the race window is small. And "a commit of its own" is most naturally read as "each edit triggers a commit", which is met.
- The cheap option: `--why` takes the path and commits only that path (`git commit -- <path>`). But that interacts with the gitleaks stage-and-reset flow and adds a mode to `take`.

Worth deciding, but it doesn't block.

**5. Test name undersells the test** (B5)
`test_a_snapshot_with_no_why_says_only_the_time` mainly checks the `why=` message, and its no-why half duplicates line 77. A rename and trim costs almost nothing.

### Noted
- **A4**: the snapshot step is a rule in prose, written in three skill files. The task asked for exactly this ("one flag and one step"). A `jbus standing add` verb would enforce it, but that is outside Where, so it is noted for later. The drift between copies is fixed by Act On 3.
- **A6 / B4**: `docs/jbus.md` is changed outside Where. The change is accurate and documents the new flag on the commands page; leaving it out would leave the flag undocumented. Keep it, and record in the review that the Where line missed this file.
- **A7**: the `with_origin` helper sits beside two older inline copies in tests the PR did not otherwise change. Folding them in is a harmless follow-up, but the scope rule keeps unchanged tests out of this PR.

### Dismissed
None. Every finding had a real basis; the ones above that aren't acted on are about cost and scope, not correctness.

### Agreement Map
The reviewers converged on the three things that matter: the missing lock, the destructive restore, and the handoff scope creep. Both traced concrete execution paths for the first two, which is the strongest signal in this review. They split on severity for the handoff duty: A called it a warning, B a nit. I side with A, because it changes who writes standing rules. A pushed the structural angle further (prose rule, whole-tree commits); B was sharper on how the two-edits-in-one-commit case defeats the undo. Neither found a problem with the `--why` flag itself or the message format. The core mechanism is sound; the gaps are in concurrency and in the safety of the documented recovery path.

  - Re-score the committed briefs. This needs no new model calls.

> The user, on the grill page: "we need to make threads more obvious per project, also i want to be able to track the work of scouts and crewmates as well." Every project's row and page gets a Threads band, grouped by role and built from `pass.json` `projects[name].threads`. A `#/<project>/thread/<role>/<slug>` route opens a drawer showing what that thread works on. The server reads one new read-only source, `scouts/` requests and their `## Report` / `Status:`, to say whether a scout is researching, reported or blocked. A pass that left no list of threads is shown as a blind spot, never as none. All of this is tested from small fixtures, with `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` green.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 7 findings
- They agreed on three issues (the duplicated row and role tables, the missing band on an empty page, the `thread/` folder outside "Where") and diverged on the rest. Both answered the review skill's questions.

### Act On

1. **An ended scout with no Report still says "researching"** (A1)
   - The chip and drawer show `q.state` ahead of liveness. A scout that crashed or was settled early therefore reads "researching" under an "ended" heading.
   - This is the exact case the user asked to be able to follow: a scout that stopped without reporting needs attention, and the page says it is still working.
   - Fix: only say researching while the thread is out. Give ended-without-Report its own word and an amber chip, and add a fixture for it.

2. **`Status: not done` shows as a green "reported"** (A2, plus B6's `Status: Blocked` case folded in)
   - `request()` maps anything other than `blocked` to `reported`, drawn with the `ok` chip. jbus's own settle check treats anything but `done` as unfinished.
   - A case-sensitive match also turns `Blocked` into "reported".
   - Fix: map `done` to reported, `blocked` to blocked and anything else to not-done, matching case-insensitively. Test a final Report whose Status is `not done`, which the current fixture never isolates.

3. **The project page draws no band when the pass listed zero threads** (A5, B2)
   - This misses the "each project's row **and page**" Done-when line.
   - The page and the row disagree on the same data.
   - Fix: delete the special case and let `band()`'s calm state handle zero. This is a deletion, not new code.

4. **The `scouts/` source always reports "ok"** (B1)
   - `seen` never passes `read` or `path`, so a missing or unreadable `scouts/` shows "ok".
   - `request()` turns every `OSError` into "missing", so a permission error makes the drawer claim the file isn't there.
   - The directory mtime also doesn't move when a Report is appended to an existing file, so `at` is a proxy that misses the event it is meant to show.
   - This is the PR's one new read-only source, and the blind-spot principle in the intent applies to it as much as to `pass.json`.
   - Fix: pass `read` and `path`, treat only `FileNotFoundError` as missing, and add a test with no `scouts/`.

5. **The thread row and the role tables are duplicated** (A3, B3)
   - `about()` in `thread/panel.js` copies `threadRow()` line for line.
   - `ROLE` (page.html) and `ROLES` (threads panel) are two positional tables that already disagree on wording ("crews" vs "Crewmates").
   - `band()` walks one table only to index into the other.
   - Both reviewers raised this independently, it is drift waiting to happen, and the inconsistency is already user-visible.
   - Direction: follow A's suggestion over B's. The drawer is a separate panel, so a shared renderer belongs in the page shell next to `threadChip`, not inside one panel that the other would have to reach into. Keep one ordered role list with named fields, and give `threadRow` a parameter for the title.

### Consider

- **The `"threads"` magic tag in `health()`** (A4 warning, B5 nit)
  - A string in a fourth tuple slot that only `projectRow` filters out, with the rule explained in prose.
  - The clean fix is small: drop the chip from `health()` and let `amber()` add its own reason.
  - Tradeoff: it touches the sidebar-dot path, which works today. It is worth doing alongside item 3, since both are about how the empty-threads fact is drawn.
- **`gates_inside=True` then re-split** (A6)
  - If the reviewer is right that plain `mirror.sections()` already stops at the gate, this is a pure deletion.
  - Tradeoff: B6 says the current form mirrors `jbus.threads._scouts`. Confirm the two produce the same body on a Report followed by `## Gate` before deleting, and add that case to the test if so.
- **`_mtime` imported across modules** (B7)
  - The B1 fix rewrites this `Source` anyway. Defining it in state.py beside `PASS_FILE` and `MERGE_LOG` costs nothing then.

### Noted

- **Unused defaults on `_threads`** (A7): minor dead branches. Make the parameters required only if no test relies on the defaults.
- **`panels/thread/` lies outside "Where"** (A8, B4)
  - The drawer is a Done-when deliverable, and the route most likely needs its own panel kind to be discovered, which explains the stub.
  - Record the reason in the PR body as "not fixed, because".
  - The undocumented `adds.band` hook belongs in `panels/__init__.py`, which is outside "Where", so it is for later.
- **One shared "last Report and its Status" helper in `jbus.threads`/`mirror`** (B6): real, but outside "Where". It is for later; the case bug is handled in item 2.

### Dismissed
None. Every finding was grounded in a concrete path. The nits were either small and real, or already covered by a merged finding.

### Agreement Map
- **Agreed:** the duplicated renderer and role tables, the missing band on an empty page, and the out-of-scope `thread/` folder. They differed only in severity, and on whether the shared code should live in the shell (A) or the panel (B).
- **Split by focus:**
  - A alone found the two scout-state correctness bugs (A1, A2), the findings that matter most for "track the work of scouts". A read the feature through the user's eyes.
  - B alone found the source-health proxy (B1) and the parse divergence (B6). B read it through the data plumbing.
- **What the pattern says:** neither reviewer padded. The structure of the UI work is sound, but the new scout-status layer was under-tested at its edges: ended with no Report, `not done`, no `scouts/` directory. Three of the five Act-on items are missing fixture cases that would each have caught their bug.

### Intent
> The audit's P7 optional items, under the user's approval of "every other upstream update." Two questions get answered from the code:
> 1. Does jmerge's "fails over today's main" check run on the merge result? If not, make it, when main changed a caller or a dependency of the PR's files (or a lockfile). Add a test.
> 2. Does a T3 launch (`modelSelection`) take an effort setting, read from T3's own tool schema? Write the decision in THIRD_PARTY.md, and keep effort at medium or lower everywhere.
>
> `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` must pass.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings (4 warnings, 3 nits)
- Reviewer B: 5 findings (4 warnings, 1 nit)
- They agreed on three issues (effort shape, bare-name imports, per-file cost) and diverged on the rest. Neither reported on the `make check` / `jgauge test-slot` lines, so those remain unconfirmed by this review.

### Act On

1. **The effort shape is asserted, not sourced, and the test can't catch a wrong one** (A1, B4).
   - The "Done when" line asks for the effort answer to be read from T3's own tool schema, and "Proves it" asks for that schema to be quoted. The fixture types `options` as `anyOf [{}, null]`, which accepts any value, so the schema says nothing about `[{"id":"effort","value":…}]`.
   - If the shape is wrong, T3 may drop the option without an error. Every Claude role would then run at the default, which is `high` by the PR's own account. That breaks the user's hard rule silently.
   - Fix: cite the real source of the shape (T3's provider or model-options code), and pin the shape in a fixture or test that fails on a different one. If no source can be found, record it as a `jbus gate`.

2. **THIRD_PARTY.md overstates the "never above medium" guarantee** (A2).
   - Codex and Grok lines send no effort, and nobody checked what those providers default to. Yet THIRD_PARTY.md and the docstring say the rule holds "for every role the map names."
   - The PR raises nothing, but the written decision is the deliverable, and it claims more than was checked.
   - Fix: narrow the wording to Claude lines and gate the Codex/Grok question. This is cheap, and it is the honest record the task asks for.

3. **An unreadable PR head fails open** (A3).
   - If `git show <head>:<path>` fails, the PR's own files read as empty, so the "main changed a dependency" direction can never match, and the check stays green.
   - Elsewhere, `cli.py` fetches `refs/pull/<n>/head` precisely because heads can be missing. In jmerge, every other git failure blocks the merge.
   - Fix: check `cat-file -e`, fetch if needed, and treat a head that still can't be read as stale. Add a test for that case.

4. **Bare-name sibling imports are missed** (A4, B2).
   - Both reviewers traced the same concrete case: about ten test files import siblings by bare name, including this PR's own `tests/test_jmerge_callers.py`. `modules()` only produces dotted paths, so a change main makes to `Kitchen` in `test_jmerge_fresh.py` never marks a dependent PR stale.
   - Fix: also name a file under the pytest import root (`tests/`) by its bare module name, and add a sibling-import test.

5. **A PR that renames a module misses callers main added under the old name** (B1).
   - `left` goes to `stale_paths` but not to `related`, and GitHub lists only the new path of a rename.
   - Moving `core.py` to `engine.py` while main adds `from pkg import core` merges a broken import. That is the core #613 scenario, and the test only covers an in-file rename.
   - Fix: pass `left` into `related` with empty text, and add a `git mv` Kitchen test.

### Consider

- **Path mentions in prose count as dependencies** (B3).
  - A PR that edits THIRD_PARTY.md or docs goes stale whenever main touches any path those files mention. This PR would be such a case.
  - It fails closed, so it is safe, but a guarded PR without `fresh-check` gets told to rebase.
  - Tradeoff: limiting path matching to executable or loaded files (code, Makefile, CI config) is a small change that removes most of the noise. Do it if the false-stale rate shows up in practice.
- **Three doc files changed outside "Where"** (A7): `docs/configuration.md`, `docs/jmerge.md`, `docs/jroles.md`.
  - The edits describe the new behaviour, and leaving them stale would be worse.
  - Keep them, but flag them in the Result so the home can confirm the scope stretch.

### Noted

- **Path substring and `conftest.py` suffix matching are loose** (A5). These fail closed and cost at most an extra check run. Tighten them if B3's fix touches `uses` anyway.
- **One `git show` per file, and O(ours×theirs) `ast.parse` calls** (A6, B5). This is consensus, but nothing shows a pass approaching the 300-second limit. `git cat-file --batch` plus parsing each file once is the remedy if one does.

### Dismissed

None. Every finding was grounded in a concrete path or a stated brief rule. The nits are low-impact, not wrong.

### Agreement Map

The reviewers converged independently on the two highest-value issues: the unproven effort shape and the missed bare-name imports. That is a strong signal on both.

Each also found a distinct fail-open hole in the new staleness check: A on an unreadable head, B on renames. Both are concrete and cheap to fix. Taken together with the bare-name gap, the dependency heuristic is under-covered in the "miss a real dependency" direction, which is the dangerous one. Its over-matching (B3, A5) only costs extra runs.

On the effort side, A went one step further than B: beyond the shape, the PR's blanket "every role" claim isn't backed for Codex or Grok.

Neither reviewer found a problem with the core decision itself, that the check now considers the merge result.

BUCKETS
A1: Act on
A2: Act on
A3: Act on
A4: Act on
A5: Noted
A6: Noted
A7: Consider
B1: Act on
B2: Act on
B3: Consider

### Intent
> Section 3 of the /deeper design: a step in the home skill's brief writing, not a separate file. It runs on its own for research, perf, analysis and outcome briefs, with its own copy of the four questions. Answer 2 goes in the scout's `Read:` or the request's sources, answer 3 in the brief for the crew, and answer 4 in `Proves it:`. Mechanical fixes, docs changes and bug fixes with a known cause skip it. `/deeper` stays manual, and `templates/brief.md`, the principle, `skills/deeper/` and the parser are untouched.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings
- Reviewer B: 7 findings
- They agreed on the two central problems, the brief lines and the playbook-keyed gate. They differed mainly on how much the request path and the tests matter. Both answered the review skill's questions.

### Act On

**1. The step writes brief lines the template forbids or never defines.** (A1, B1)
The step tells the home to put answer 2 in `Read:` and answer 3 in `Instruments:`.
- `templates/brief.md:17` says a home-written brief leaves `Read:` out.
- `Instruments:` exists nowhere outside this diff. The template, the crew skill, the scout skill and the parser don't define it.
- So the scout drops answer 3 by following its own skill, and a home that reads the template first gets the opposite instruction.
- The phrase "though the home wrote it" names the clash without resolving it.

The intent only asks for `Read:` on the *scout's* brief, so the home-brief `Read:` instruction overreaches the task. Fix inside "Where":
- Drop `Instruments:`.
- Send answer 3 to a line that already exists, such as the Done-when list or the task body.
- Keep `Read:` to scout-written briefs.

If a dedicated line is still wanted, the Result notes `templates/brief.md` and the scout skill as a follow-up. Both are outside "Where".

**2. The gate keys on the playbook name, not the kind of work.** (A2, A3, A4, B2, B3; merged)
This is one design flaw with three symptoms, each on a concrete path:
- **`bug-fix` always skips.** That playbook exists to root-cause bugs whose cause is unknown. The boundary only exempts known-cause fixes, and the test locks the mismatch in under a "known bug" label.
- **Outcome work skips whenever a playbook is picked**, for example `feature`, `autonomous-run` or `swarm`. The intent asks for the step on outcome briefs.
- **Every scout request runs the step.** Scouts only run `investigation` or `trace-forensics`, which are both in the arm, even when the brief being requested is for a docs change or a known-cause fix. That breaks the second "Done when" line.
- **The hand-kept list drifts.** It holds ten playbook names, and the test only checks one direction (each name is a file).

The fix is to make the stated kind of the *task being briefed* the input, for example `research|perf|analysis|outcome|known-cause-fix|mechanical|docs`. The playbook name then decides nothing. The fix lives in `skills/home/SKILL.md` and its test. It deletes the list rather than patching it, and resolves all five findings together.

### Consider

- **Requests whose "Deliver" asks for no brief lose answers 3 and 4.** (A5, B4) B's remedy is cheap and uses lines the template already has: write 3 and 4 as `Questions:` items in the request. It also replaces the awkward packing of 3 and 4 into the single Deliver bullet. The case is real but narrow. Do it if you're rewriting that sentence for finding 1 anyway.
- **A test that the brief lines the step names exist in `templates/brief.md`.** (A6) It is cheap and would have caught finding 1. It also executes something (reads the template and checks it), which makes it worth more than another text match.
- **Fold the "Done when already names its data, instruments and judge" skip into the block's input.** (B6) Once the input is the kind of work (Act On 2), this is one more value rather than a prose override the home must remember after seeing the questions printed. Low cost if done alongside 2.
- **"The block under it" at SKILL.md:430 points 90 lines away into another section.** (B5) A one-line clarity fix. Name the section.

### Noted

- **`make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` are unverified.** (B7) The reviewer ran nothing by instruction, so this is not a defect in the change. Both "Done when" lines still have to be run and reported, with output, in the Result before merge.
- **"Proves it" needs one post-merge brief carrying the four answers.** Not raised by either reviewer, but it follows from the intent. The Result must say how the home will check that brief.

### Dismissed

- **A4/B3's alternative: a marker in each playbook's `Run by:` row.** It is outside "Where" and made unnecessary once the gate keys on kind, so it should not be logged as a follow-up either. The finding itself is covered under Act On 2.

### Agreement Map

The reviewers converged independently on the two structural problems: the brief lines that don't exist or are forbidden, and the playbook-keyed gate. That consensus, backed by concrete execution paths (`picked='bug-fix'` prints the known-cause skip), is why both are Act On.

A alone traced the scout-request path (A3) and showed it is the same root cause as the bug-fix and outcome misses. That is what lets five findings collapse into one fix. B was more thorough on the request side (B4, B5, B6) and on unverified "Done when" lines. Neither inflated style nits.

The pattern says the step's prose is close, but its mechanism (the case arm) and its destinations (the brief lines) were designed against the wrong inputs. Fixing those two makes most of the remaining findings fall away.

### Intent
> Task: the audit's P6. Once a crewmate has written `fixed and green`, it does not make a third rebase forced by main. It writes one stop line in its Result and pipes a gate, and jbus surfaces it as waiting. The count is kept where jbus or jmerge can read it. A suite test drives three rebases and finds the stop on the third. `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` pass. Where: `skills/crew/SKILL.md` ("A conflict"), `src/jmerge/` or `src/jbus/`, the tests. Do not touch how a rebase is pushed.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings (3 warnings, 3 nits)
- Reviewer B: 5 findings (4 warnings, 1 nit)
- Both reviewers raised the same two issues independently: the jbus step mapping and the `Fixed:` stand-in. They also overlapped on test coverage of jmerge's `waits()` path. The review skill's questions were asked; both reviewers worked from them.
- Neither reviewer reported on the `make check` / `jgauge test-slot` "Done when" line. Confirm it before merge.

### Act On

1. **The held pull request maps to the `rebase` step ("its crewmate") when it waits on the user.** Raised by A1 and B1.
   - Location: `src/jbus/merge.py:97`, pinned by `tests/test_jbus_merge.py:288`.
   - Once the gate is answered or never parked, nothing outranks the step. The board then says "Rebase, its crewmate" for good, while the crewmate is forbidden to rebase.
   - This contradicts the PR's own SKILL text ("waiting on the user"). It also cuts against the repo's existing pattern: `NOT_UPHELD` and `UNRULED_DROPS` map to `hold`.
   - The fix is one rule and one test entry: move the reason to `hold`.

2. **Running the block twice parks a duplicate gate.** Raised by A3.
   - Location: `skills/crew/SKILL.md:86-87, 118`.
   - The path is concrete. `mainmoved.py` wakes red PRs on every main commit, and a held PR is often red. Each wake reprints `hold:`, and the prose says to park a gate on `hold`.
   - This is the run-twice/reconciliation case the review asks about.
   - The fix is cheap: print a distinct word such as `held:` when the line already exists, and park the gate only on the first `hold:`.

3. **The count reads the whole brief, not the last Result.** Raised by B2.
   - Location: `skills/crew/SKILL.md:396-399`.
   - SKILL.md:159 sets the rule that every block reads the last result. With the current awk, a follow-up round inherits the old `Rebased after fixed:` lines and is held on its first conflict.
   - Resetting the counters on `/^## Result/` fixes it and keeps the block consistent with every other block.

4. **The jmerge reading path and the conflict-counting path are untested.** Raised by A5 and B4.
   - The proves-it test does drive three rebases through the real shell block, which meets the "Done when" line. But two paths go unexecuted:
     - the `waits()` change at `cli.py:703`: its ordering before `short_of` and its early return;
     - the `counted` call in the stopped-rebase branch (SKILL.md:443).
   - Either could be deleted and the suite would stay green. The `waits()` path is how "jbus surfaces it as waiting" is actually delivered, so it needs an executing test.
   - Add both:
     - a `waits()` (or jmerge `wait` line → `merge.step`) assertion on a brief holding at the head;
     - a run where main touches the branch's own file, so the rebase stops and is still counted.

### Consider

- **`Fixed:` stands in for "fixed and green".** Raised by A2 and B3.
  - This is a real proxy. `Fixed:` is written right after the push, and `Fixed: none needed` starts the count too. Rebases while CI is red can therefore use up the cap early.
  - Against that, the PR explains its reason: `fixed and green` is sent to the home, not written to the brief. A new green marker would mean a new writer and a new convention in the crew flow, which is more than an S-sized task should grow.
  - Erring early is the safe direction for a churn cap. A gate is cheap; an endless rebase loop is not.
  - Minimum: state the deviation from the "Done when" line explicitly in the PR so the home can rule on it. Add a green marker only if the home wants the literal condition.
- **The hold is recorded at local `HEAD`; jmerge compares it with GitHub's head.** Raised by A4.
  - The path is real but narrow: a refused push followed by another main move. Even then, the gate still reaches the user; only the jmerge reason is wrong.
  - The fix is nearly free, because the block already has `pushed` from `gh pr view`. Worth taking while the block is open for item 2.

### Noted

- **The block's de-dup disagrees with `rebase_held`.** Raised by B5.
  - The de-dup accepts any earlier hold line at that head; `rebase_held` uses the last hold-or-lift line.
  - It is valid, but it needs a lift, a stopped rebase, and a return to the exact same head.
  - If item 2's fix rewrites that grep anyway, match `rebase_held`'s last-line rule while there.

### Dismissed

- **The test helper's `home` argument also switches the slug.** Raised by A6.
  - The helper has one caller, and the risk named is a hypothetical future caller.
  - Generalising the test helper now would be premature.

### Agreement Map

The reviewers converged on what matters: the jbus mapping and the proxy. Each was raised independently and with the same evidence, which is a strong signal.

They diverged usefully on the rest:
- A focused on run-twice and head-identity hazards (A3, A4).
- B focused on the scope of what the awk reads and on untested branches (B2, B4).

Neither reviewer padded with style nits; their nits name concrete paths. Together the findings say the mechanism is sound and well-tested at the shell level. Its two edges are not: the jbus/jmerge surfacing and the block's idempotence across wakes and rounds. Those edges are where the four Act On items sit, and all four are small.

### Intent
> Section 4 of the /deeper design: "a new brief field: `Proves it:` in `templates/brief.md`, right after `Done when:`. The brief parser requires it to name something outside the agent: a test, metric, dataset, external judge or the user. It rejects "reviewed by crewmate", "reviewed by reviewer", and empty or self-referential answers."

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 7 findings (3 warnings, 4 nits)
- Reviewer B: 6 findings (1 critical, 2 warnings, 3 nits)
- The two agreed on four points: the loose `_OUTSIDE` patterns, the duplicated head loop, the unused `Brief.proof`, and the `<` template check. Only A raised the grandfathering hole and the double gate. Only B raised the gap in test coverage.

### Act On

**1. The `_OUTSIDE` patterns accept self-referential lines, and they are checked first** (A1, B1; tests: B2)
- `proof()` returns success on the first `_OUTSIDE` match and never reaches `_SELF`.
- Several patterns are bare keywords, so these lines all launch as "outside":
  - "make sure the reviewer is happy"
  - "self-test"
  - `` `the crewmate` checks it ``
  - "the reviewer is 100% sure"
  - "the model is the judge"
  - "the agent's own eval"
- This is the only gate before `_ready` launches. So the Done-when line "refuses a proof by the crew, the crewmate, the reviewer, the agent, self, the model" is not met in practice.
- Both reviewers traced concrete inputs independently, so this is the strongest signal in the review.
- Fix:
  - A test counts only as a path (`tests/…`, `test_\w+`) or a backticked command that starts with a known tool (`make <target>`, `uv`, `pytest`, `jbus`, `jgauge`).
  - `%` counts only next to a metric word.
  - `judge` counts only when the subject is not a `_SELF` word.
  - Drop "his word/pick/eye", or tie them to "the user".
  - Add every example above to `REFUSED`, so the precedence rule is tested on its failing side as well as its passing side (B2).

**2. A missing `Proves it:` line is exempt forever, not only on briefs queued before the change** (A2)
- `proven()` returns `""` whenever `proves_it` returns None. Nothing ties that to when the row was approved.
- Result: a brief written tomorrow without the line launches with no gate.
- The requirement then lives only in the home skill's prose. That is the "rule in prose" case question 4 warns about, and it defeats "the parser requires it".
- The Done-when line asked for a choice that "does not strand an approved row". It did not ask for a standing exemption.
- Fix: grandfather only rows whose `approved` time is before this change's cut-off (the queue already records it), and gate a missing line on anything approved later.

### Consider

**3. Design and proof faults raise two gates in sequence** (A3; also covers B3's `_ready` branch)
- When a brief fails both checks, the user fixes the design, re-approves, and only then sees the proof gate.
- Every round is a re-approval by the user, and the fix is small: collect both faults, join them, and send one gate keyed by the brief sha.
- That also replaces the `short, kind` juggling with a loop over `(kind, check)` pairs.
- Tradeoff: one more change to `_ready`, inside the Where line, for fewer user round-trips.

**4. Detect the template's text by exact match, not a leading `<`** (A6, B5)
- Two errors follow from the `<` test:
  - A real line such as `<= 50 ms p95 from jgauge` is refused as template text.
  - The guide text with its brackets removed is accepted, because it contains "test".
- `templates/brief.md` is the one copy, so compare against its line with the brackets stripped, or use `^<[^>]*>$`.
- Cheap, and it makes the "refuses the template line" test exact. Fix 1 removes part of the risk, but not the false refusal.

### Noted

### Intent
> Every gate becomes act-unless-stopped. The thread acts on its default at once, the user is shown the gate as already acted on, and a differing answer is carried back. A gate whose default deletes data, rewrites history, spends money, touches prod or real users, changes access or secrets, or publishes must say `Holds: <case>` and name a `Fail-safe:`. Such a gate does not act, waits for the user with the fail-safe attached, and is never closed by silence. `jbus gate` refuses a gate with no default, with a recommended option that is not the default, with an unknown case, or with a `Holds:` and no fail-safe. A pass closes plain open questions after 2 hours by silence, on a basis that says it is not the user's word. A later differing answer is still taken. The skills, the template and the docs state the rule and the table, all in this one PR, with fake-clock tests and `make check` green.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 6 findings
- Reviewer B: 6 findings

1. **A silence-closed question re-piped with `Holds:` replies "already answered", and the thread goes ahead** (A1)
   - Since silence now sets `answer`, `ask` treats a silence-closed record as settled and discards any new `Holds:`/`Fail-safe:` lines.
   - A thread that later learns its default deletes data, and re-pipes with `Holds: deletes data`, is told to "go by it". Nobody said yes.

2. **A `Holds:` gate answered `--default` (or ticked on the page) never reaches its thread** (B1)
   - `tell` and `View._carry` skip `keeps` answers on the old assumption that the default was already done.
   - For a held gate it wasn't, so "yes, do the recommended thing" leaves the action parked forever. Only a differing answer moves it.
   - This breaks the core of the held path. No test answers a held gate at all.
   - Fix: carry a "go ahead with the default" message when `holds` is set. Make `_answer` and the docs (docs/jbus.md:132) say so. Add a test showing that `--default` on a held gate sends exactly one message.

### Intent
> Sections 1, 2, 5 and 6 of the /deeper design, built on Felix Rieseberg's "four types of ambition" (Depth). The work has four parts:
> - **The skill.** A manual-only `skills/deeper/` returns the four answers and a rewritten prompt. Run by a home, it does not block: the rewrite becomes the default and goes to a `jbus gate`.
> - **The principle.** `principles/depth-over-breadth.md` is the 25th principle. jdrift lists it as a jstack source, and every count of principles says 25.
> - **The credit.** `THIRD_PARTY.md` credits Rieseberg and ties the credit to the planned pstack port.
> - **The eval.** A blind, rerunnable eval in `evals/deeper/` uses about 10 past briefs. It scores raw sources, instruments named, and whether the proof is outside the agent. Its result is reported honestly, and a loss is a finding, not a reason to tune.
>
> `make check` and `jgauge test-slot -- make check` pass.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 5 findings
- Reviewer B: 8 findings
- They agreed on two issues: the raw measure copying the skill's own list, and `write()` deleting the committed runs before any model call. Each also raised a separate, complementary problem with the eval's verdict. The review skill's questions were asked of both.

### Act On

1. **The "won" verdict is not supported on proof outside (A1, B1, merged).** The rule requires no loss on any measure, so the verdict depends entirely on the "outside" measure. Two independent reasons say that measure does not show a win:
   - **A1:** Any backtick span counts as an outside judge. With that branch removed, the two arms are level: 0.34 for plain, 0.33 for deeper. A rescored the committed briefs to show this.
   - **B1:** Run 1 lost on outside. The only change before run 2 was the output format of the rewrite, a fence turned into a block quote. Outside then flipped sign on 8 of 10 cases. That is noise, and the README's own "only what the two runs agree on" rule excludes it.

   The task says plainly that a loss is a finding and not a reason to tune. This is the eval's central claim, so it blocks.
   - **Fix:**
     - Restrict the backtick branch to commands that are run, or drop it.
     - Rescore the committed briefs. This needs no model calls.
     - Restate the Result as: won on raw and instruments in both runs; proof outside not shown.
     - Drop the README's claim that `Proves it:` is "aimed at that gap" unless the rescore supports it.

2. **The raw measure largely counts the skill's own example list (A2, B2).** Both reviewers found this independently. Seven of the twelve `RAW` kinds match the words of question 2 almost exactly. The README says the effect holds "not only by copying the skill's own examples", but only instruments have a `beyond` control.
   - **Fix:** Add a raw `beyond` that leaves out the skill's listed kinds and rescore. Otherwise, narrow the sentence to instruments. Either way it is cheap and needs no model calls.

3. **The one rerun command destroys the committed results if it fails (A3, B3).** Both reviewers found this independently. `write()` runs `rmtree` on `runs/` and `deeper/` before 60 `claude -p` calls. It does this even when `claude` is not installed. `key.json` is written only at the end, so any failure leaves a partial `runs/` and a stale key, and recovery needs git. "Rerunnable by one command" is a "Done when" line, and this is the crash-halfway case.
   - **Fix:** Write into a temporary directory and swap it in once the key is written. Also check `shutil.which("claude")` before deleting anything.

4. **Redaction silently turns off when the patterns do not load (B4).** Only one reviewer raised this, but it is a privacy issue in a repo meant to be public:
   - `_private` ignores `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, although `jleak`'s own CLI respects it.
   - It also swallows `jleak.Missing` and returns no patterns.

   Text from the private task store is then committed unredacted.
   - **Fix:**
     - Resolve the config path the way `jleak.cli` does.
     - Fail hard in `cases` and `write` when the patterns are missing.
     - Check that the briefs already committed were in fact redacted.

5. **The principle card lists playbooks that do not use the principle (B6).** The leans field names `perf-issue` and `investigation`, but neither playbook links to depth-over-breadth. The card is rendered on the explained page, so the page states something false. The fix is one line within Where: list only `deeper`. Linking the playbooks is outside Where and is for later.

### Intent
> Make threads obvious per project and let the user follow scouts and crewmates. Each project's row and page gets a Threads band by role (crewmates, scouts, reviewers, home): threads that are out come first with liveness and last write, threads ended today are dimmed, and the rest are folded. The data comes from `pass.json` `projects[name].threads`. `#/<project>/thread/<role>/<slug>` opens a drawer showing what the thread works on. The server reads one new read-only source, each scout request's `## Report` and `Status:` under `scouts/`, to say researching, reported or blocked. A pass with no list of threads is shown as a blind spot, never as none. All of this is tested from small fixtures, and `make check` passes, both directly and under `jgauge test-slot`.

### Reviewers
- Reviewer A: 8 findings
- Reviewer B: 7 findings
- They agreed on four issues: the empty-list band, the duplicated row and role tables, the `health()` tag, and the `thread/` folder. Each found correctness bugs in the scout status that the other missed. Both answered the review skill's questions.

1. **An ended scout with no Report still reads "researching"** (A1). `request()` derives state from the file alone, and `threadChip` puts that state ahead of liveness. A crashed or interrupted scout therefore looks busy, which is the one case the user most needs to see. Only say researching while the thread is out. Give an ended scout with no Report its own word on an amber chip, and add a fixture for it.
2. **`Status: not done` is shown as a green "reported"** (A2, plus the concrete half of B6). Anything other than `blocked` maps to `ok`. jbus's own settle check treats anything but `done` as unfinished, so the view says "finished" when jbus says "not". Map `done` to reported, `blocked` to blocked, and anything else to a non-`ok` not-done state, matched case-insensitively (`Blocked` currently reads as reported). Test a final Report whose status is `not done`.
3. **The `scouts/` source can never be anything but "ok"** (B1). `seen` passes neither `read` nor `path`, so `_source` can't say missing or unreadable. `request()` also turns every `OSError` into "missing", so a permission error tells the user the file doesn't exist. - Reviewer B: 8 findings

- A1 showed that the whole plain-to-deeper rise in "outside" comes from the backtick branch of `OUTSIDE` (`evals/deeper/score.py`). Without that branch the two arms are level (0.34 vs 0.33).

- Why it matters: the task's own "Done when" requires the Result to say faithfully whether /deeper won.
- Fix:
  - Drop or narrow the backtick branch, so a span counts only when it holds a run command.
  - Rescore the committed briefs. This needs no model calls.
  - Restate the Result from what both runs agree on.
- This is correcting a measure, not tuning toward a win. If the honest answer becomes "won on raw and instruments, outside not shown, rule not met", that is the finding to report.

  - "make sure the reviewer is happy"
  - "self-test"
  - "`the crewmate` checks it"
  - "the reviewer is 100% sure"
  - "the model is the judge"
- Refusing exactly these is the core of the task. The gate is the only thing between such a line and a launch, so this is a correctness bug, not a hypothetical.
- The "a test the crewmate runs is still a test" precedence is right, but only when the outside match really names a test.

  - Tighten the patterns: a path or `test_` name, a backticked span that starts with a known tool, `make <target>` but not "make sure", and `%` only near a metric word.

- The Done-when asks to grandfather *existing queued* briefs so no approved row is stranded. It does not ask for a permanent bypass.

### Act On

**1. Snapshots have no lock, so they now race each other and the timer** (A1, B1)
- Before this change, `take` had one caller twice a day. Now any home can call it at any moment against the same index.
- Both reviewers traced concrete paths, not hypotheticals:
  - **Lock collision:** two runs collide on `.git/index.lock`. If the timer loses, `OnFailure` fires `--alarm` and alerts every project about a failure that isn't real.
  - **Reset race:** one home's `git reset -q` runs between another home's `add` and `diff --cached`. The second home prints "nothing changed", and its edit never gets its own commit. That breaks the main "Done when" line.
- The fix is small and inside Where: an exclusive `flock` on a file in the tree's `.git`, held across add, commit and push in `take`.
- Add a test that holds the lock and shows a second `take` waits rather than fails.

**2. The documented restore empties the live `standing.md` when `git show` fails** (A2, B2)
- The shell truncates the target before `git show` runs.
- `git show` fails in ordinary cases: a mistyped hash, undoing the edit that created the file, or the root commit. Each leaves an empty rules file, and the doc's very next step snapshots it.
- This is a correctness bug in the exact recovery path the task exists to provide.
- Fix: document `git -C ~/.local/state/home restore --source=<commit>^ -- <repo>/standing.md`. It writes nothing on failure.
- Say what to do when the bad edit created the file.
- Test the case where the parent has no such file.

**3. The handoff skill gains a duty to write standing rules** (A5, B3)
- "One it did not write yet goes there now" adds a new place where rules get written.
- It contradicts the sentence before it ("the home wrote it to `standing.md` when it heard it").
- It doesn't trace to the task. The task asked handoff to snapshot after its edits, not to start making edits.
- Cut it and keep only the general instruction: after any edit to `$H/standing.md`, run `jbus snapshot --why ...`.
- This is cheap, and it stops a behaviour change from slipping in under a "one flag and one step" design.

### Consider

**4. A `--why` commit sweeps the whole dirty tree under a message that names only `standing.md`** (A3, and B1's "mixed commits" and "two edits in one commit" points)

- Committing only the named path when `--why` is given (`git commit -- <path>`) would make the message true and the commit truly "of its own".

Every edit a home or a handoff makes to `$H/standing.md` is followed right away by `jbus snapshot`, so it lands as its own pushed commit in `~/.local/state/home`. The twice-daily timer stays. `jbus snapshot --why <text>` puts the reason after the timestamp in the commit message. `docs/state.md` documents how to find an edit with `log -p`, restore it with `show <commit>^:...`, and snapshot again. ### Act On

**1. No lock around `take` now that snapshots run at any time (A1, B1)**
- Before this change, only the timer called `take`. Now any home, scoped homes included, can run `git add -A` → `commit` → `push` on the same index at any moment.

- A1's second path is also concrete. One run's `git reset -q`, which happens on a gitleaks hit or when gitleaks is missing, can wipe another run's staging. That edit then gets "nothing changed" and no commit, which defeats the "commit of its own" line.

- Reviewer B: 8 findings

`_filled` (`src/jbriefs/parse.py:355`) treats a value as template text only when it starts with `<`. Four of the template's own lines don't:
- `"<…>"` starts with a quote.
- `- <a check>` starts with a list marker.
- `open one when done | ask first` has no `<`.
- `review | none` has no `<`.

So a brief copied straight from `templates/brief.md` passes `queue add` on those four fields. The existing test writes `Task: <the request>` without the quotes, so it never sees the gap.

Stripping the apostrophe (`meaning.py:94`) turns `shouldn't` into `shouldnt`. That is two edits from `should` with both words five letters or more, so `_near` pairs them. The result: "the gate should fire" changed to "the gate shouldn't fire" keeps the user's approval.

The two-edit rule is in the spec. Joining contractions is the author's own choice, and it is exactly what puts a negation inside the allowance. That defeats "still catching real changes to intent or scope" in the most dangerous direction.

- Split `n't` into a separate `not` token.
- Add a test showing `should` changed to `shouldn't` re-asks.
- State the residual limits the spec does imply in `docs/jbus.md` and the PR body: near antonyms such as `include`/`exclude`, and direction lost to filler-dropping plus sorting ("move `a.py` to `b.py`"). A check added later to `dispatch` would gate at launch and pass at `add`, which is the bug this task fixes. The one parity test covers only Design.

- **The PR says the launch checks are unchanged, but `playbook` now refuses non-crewmate playbooks** (A8). The behaviour is what the task asked for. The PR description should say so, since rows approved since `shaped_since` with such a playbook will now gate at launch.

The reviewers converged independently on the three Act On items: the template-text hole, contraction negation, and check drift. They also both flagged the `endswith` coupling. That consensus on concrete execution paths is the strongest signal in the review.
